query: FeCoNi is an fcc alloy with high saturation magnetization and a low coercive field. Earlier studies examined the high-entropy alloys FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt, but both exhibited soft ferromagnetism. A qualifying high-entropy alloy must have an almost equiatomic multicomponent composition and configurational entropy of at least 1.0R. Subject to these constraints, what single intervention could produce a FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy with greater coercivity than the prior derivatives? Present one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an appropriate FeCoNi-based baseline, defines the conditions over which it should apply, cites supporting observations from earlier work, and proposes a discriminating experiment with an explicit falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating 1–2 at.% interstitial carbon into a nearly equiatomic FeCoNi fcc high‐entropy alloy will significantly increase its coercivity relative to the carbon‐free baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: A nearly equiatomic, high-entropy FeCoNi alloy with an fcc structure, exhibiting high saturation magnetization but low coercivity (as observed in FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt derivatives).
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled 1–2 at.% addition of interstitial carbon into the alloy during processing.
generation.conditions: The carbon must be uniformly distributed without forming carbide precipitates, preserving the overall fcc structure and configurational entropy above 1.0R. The processing (e.g., melting followed by rapid quenching) should ensure homogeneous interstitial incorporation.
generation.structural_mediator: Interstitial carbon atoms that occupy sites in the fcc lattice, creating localized lattice distortions.
generation.mechanism: The presence of interstitial carbon induces local lattice strain, resulting in regions of enhanced magnetocrystalline anisotropy. These distorted regions act as pinning centers for magnetic domain walls, thereby hindering their motion and increasing the coercive field.
generation.predicted_outcome: The carbon-doped FeCoNi alloy will exhibit a significantly increased coercive field relative to the carbon-free baseline, while maintaining high saturation magnetization.
generation.baseline: The original FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy without interstitial carbon (or with noble metal additions such as Pd or Pt that yield soft ferromagnetism).
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies under processing conditions that maintain the fcc crystal structure and high configurational entropy. Excess carbon that leads to carbide formation or disrupts the structure would fall outside the hypothesis scope.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of the increase in coercivity is uncertain without experimental calibration; additionally, the optimal carbon content within the 1–2 at.% window may vary based on processing specifics.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples using otherwise identical processing parameters: one set of the baseline equiatomic FeCoNi high-entropy alloy and another set with an added 1–2 at.% carbon. Ensure that both sets maintain the fcc structure and high configurational entropy. Perform standardized room-temperature magnetic hysteresis measurements on both sets.
measurements: Magnetic hysteresis loops to determine coercive field values.
Structural analysis (e.g., X-ray diffraction) to confirm the fcc phase and detect any carbide precipitates.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the carbon-doped alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant increase in coercivity beyond experimental uncertainty compared to the baseline sample, or if carbon addition leads to phase changes (e.g., carbide formation) that compromise the fcc structure and high-entropy criteria, then the hypothesis is falsified.

frame.system: A FeCoNi-based fcc high‐entropy alloy that in its baseline state is nearly equiatomic with high saturation magnetization but low coercivity (as seen in variants like FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt which are soft ferromagnets).
frame.goal: To obtain an equiatomic, high-entropy FeCoNi-based alloy that exhibits a significantly higher coercive field by a single compositional or processing intervention.
frame.limitation: Prior derivative alloys (e.g., FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt) produced low coercivity (i.e. soft ferromagnetism) despite satisfying high configurational entropy constraints, indicating that mere addition of noble metals is not enough to generate hard magnetic behaviour.
constraints: The alloy must be almost equiatomic with multiple principal elements.
The configurational entropy must be at least 1.0R.
Any intervention must be a single change (i.e. a single compositional or processing modification) relative to the baseline.
frame.regime: Standard room-temperature magnetic measurements (hysteresis loops) under applied magnetic fields, with the alloy processed under conditions that preserve the fcc crystal structure.
prior_attempts: Inclusion of Pd and Pt in FeCoNi alloys has been attempted, but these yielded soft ferromagnetic behaviour (low coercivity) rather than hard magnetic response.
frame.understanding: While prior work indicates that adding noble metals does not strengthen coercivity, it is hypothesized that a microstructural intervention which introduces controlled lattice distortions could enhance magnetocrystalline anisotropy and pinning of domain walls, thereby increasing coercivity.
frame.proposed_intervention: Introduce an interstitial element—specifically, add a controlled minor amount of carbon—to the FeCoNi matrix. Carbon atoms occupy interstitial sites in the fcc lattice, locally distorting the lattice and enhancing anisotropy fields. This distortion acts as a pinning centre for magnetic domain walls, thereby increasing the coercive field compared to the carbon‐free baseline.
frame.mechanism: The interstitial carbon creates local lattice strains and potentially induces nanoscale regions of non‐uniform magnetic anisotropy. These regions serve as effective pinning sites that hinder domain wall motion, resulting in an increase of the coercivity. This mechanism builds on earlier observations in steels and certain high-entropy systems where interstitial doping improves magnetic hardness.
frame.predicted_outcome: Under otherwise identical processing and composition constraints, the FeCoNi alloy with a minor carbon addition (e.g., approximately 1–2 atomic % C) will show a significantly increased coercive field relative to the baseline FeCoNi alloy or even to the variants with Pd/Pt addition, while maintaining high saturation magnetization.
frame.applicable_conditions: This intervention should be effective when the carbon is added in controlled amounts that do not disrupt the overall fcc structure or reduce the configurational entropy below 1.0R. The processing route (e.g., melting and rapid quenching) must be chosen to ensure a homogeneous distribution of carbon interstitials without forming carbide precipitates.
frame.supporting_observations: Similar effects have been observed in carbon-doped steels and in other interstitially-modified magnetic alloys where small atoms induce strain and locally enhance magnetic anisotropy. Prior studies in high-entropy alloys have also indicated that controlled lattice distortions can tune magnetic properties.
frame.discriminating_experiment: Prepare two sets of alloys: one set of standard FeCoNi (or a nominal equiatomic baseline alloy meeting high-entropy criteria) and another set with an additional 1–2 at.% carbon under identical processing conditions. Measure the magnetic hysteresis loops for both sets at room temperature. The hypothesis is falsified if the carbon-doped alloy does not display a statistically significant increase in coercivity (e.g., an increase beyond experimental uncertainty relative to the baseline) despite the controlled intervention.

In this case, adding a minor interstitial element (carbon) introduces local lattice distortions that act as pinning centers for magnetic domain walls.
